utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. May I remind you, ambassador, of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Okun, we shall now continue our cross-examination. I went through yesterday's transcript and there is a detail there that I didn't quite understand. I will be going back to that. I know it will probably be difficult for you to remember every single detail from long ago. I shall try to refresh your memory. I read yesterday's transcript. I'll ask you some questions about the timeline which to me is essential. Surely you understand that it's very important for me to pin down -- to pinpoint certain events. On page 27 of the transcript, and on page 65, I asked you when in your estimate the event took place that we saw in the footage. You said between 1230 hours and 1300 hours. Before that, you said that the other event was between 12.40 and 12.45. Now, that doesn't seem totally. What we saw on the screen, was that before what happened with the rifle and how much time had elapsed between the two? If you can specify, please. So the conversation that we saw on the video and the rifle incident, as it were.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could clarify that, of course, not to the minute. We weren't there with a stopwatch. The entire visit lasted, it's recorded -- as recorded in my diary notes from 11 a.m. To 1 p.m. The -- and we were driving around and stopping and visiting. So there was driving, there was visits to places like the JNA barracks, the refugee camp that you've discussed, and then we stopped also just to get out of the APCs and look around. You mentioned yesterday going to a hilltop to get a view of the city with binoculars which I didn't recall because we were driving. Now, the video that we saw showed us, I believe, entering the city because you could see the houses were rather small and it wasn't really an urban settlement. You might refer to it as a -- suburban but wasn't -- you know, the city. And so we drove in and we got out. We alighted and visited the JNA barracks and I've described that. I told you we were there for, you know, 15 minutes, perhaps more, perhaps less. We drove around more to see the town, a lot. I noted that's reported in my diary where I say in the diary, just to recall our memory for the Court, "much of town seen nonetheless." You see, much of the town. So this was driving. And we then drove to the -- we visited the refugee centre. We spent some time there and it was -- now, remember, Major Sljivancanin was with us for almost all of this time. We didn't see him every second because he was obviously in his own military vehicle. But as I've already described to you yesterday, in answer to your questions, once he appeared on the scene, as it was clear he was the senior officer present with us, and was what we call -- would call an escort officer, the escort officer, so that he and Mr. Vance then maintained what I described yesterday to you as a running dialogue. That is to say they didn't have just one separate conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please let me finish. Please, let me finish. I'm almost finished. They had several conversations and, as I reported to you yesterday, as Mr. Vance kept asking to see the hospital and as we neared the hospital, the conversations became first an argument, then an altercation, and finally a shouting match, where -- and at that point, it was at that point, the climax of the obstruction that Major Sljivancanin actually raised a weapon. So I hope that gives you the timeline.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I've heard all of that already but what I haven't heard is an answer to my question. Can you please specify how much time elapsed between what we see in the video and this final moment? Could you specify that in terms of time, please?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin's lecture that we actually saw where he was saying, standing and giving his little speech to us? Because we saw him more than once. That's my point, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, then, maybe this is a good time to go back to the video which I was going to do any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the first time the Defence teams are using this new technology. That's one thing I need to say at the outset. My case manager will now be doing what we are actually used to the technical services doing for us. Can we now please show the portion of the video that we saw? And if the Chamber wishes to follow the transcript, which I have challenged, this is 69, although perhaps it will be better to just watch the video. However, I would like to have a hard copy placed in front of Mr. Okun. A brief portion of that video or rather the dialogue. That is what we shall now be revisiting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, I marked the page that refers to this portion of the video. If you could please watch the footage and follow the transcript at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now go back to my previous question. This is the dialogue that I'm interested in, the exchange. You're quite right; there were several scenes that were shown. But this is the first exchange that we see as proof that a visit to the hospital was being discussed. You testified in chief that there had been conversations before this point in time and Mr. Vance was already angry. Can you specify how much time elapsed between this point in time shown on the video and the rifle incident?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Approximately. You can hear Mr. Vance quite angry at the very end of the video, saying, let's go downtown, because he had already asked to visit the hospital. He did that many times and the answer was always negative. We heard Major Sljivancanin giving this excuse about the mines. So we then travelled more around town and stopped and, you know, there was another conversation, stopped. So there was probably -- 11.00, we entered, we drove in 11.15, the barracks, 11.30. This was all happening between 12, 12.15, maybe even 12.30, and 1 p.m. As I said there was a running conversation being maintained and this was part of it but near the climax because you can see Mr. Vance very angry, you can see major Sljivancanin lecturing him and telling him in no uncertain terms that it was impossible to reach the hospital. So this was towards the end of their shouting match.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course, I can't question the fact that you knew Mr. Vance very well. My understanding is you were more than colleagues, you were friends, even partners. In this footage, you claim that you see him very angry, based on your familiarity with him. Can you please confirm that, sir?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very definitely. You can see it on his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, after this, you went to the place where the incident occurred. You testified in chief that there was a square right in the middle of the town. You could see bridges from there and you could see a roof which you were told at the time was the roof of the hospital. This is what you said two days ago, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said we were in open area. I said a small square. It could have been round. It was an open area where streets intersect. I mean that's -- you know, the town, Mr. Lukic, you have to understand, was thoroughly destroyed, so that the driving around, one didn't get exactly the picture. It wasn't The Hague, you know, where you know where streets meet. We were in a shattered city, the likes of which I had never seen, so there was rubble around us and destroyed vehicles, that sort of thing. I remember it was very sunny. The sun had come out at that point, at the final -- at the climax with the weapon, and that was as close as we got to the hospital, and I've described that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said you saw something that were you told was the hospital roof; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- we were told, yes, we were told there is the bridge. We never crossed the bridge, you see. We never reached the hospital so I can only recount what we were told. Now, whether it was accurate or not is not for me to say since we were denied passage to the hospital, we were denied passage across the bridge. We were stopped, held, at that point. We went no further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please just tell me, am I wrong on this one? My client submits, and so do I since I was there, that Vukovar is a town in the plains and that if you stand at a point anywhere inside the town, there is no way you can see the hospital roof across the river and that the bridges can only be seen if you're standing right next to them. There is no single location right there in the middle of town or a square from which you could see the bridges. Would I be wrong in stating my case in this way?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a flat town that is the east -- Eastern Slavonia is an agricultural area. I would not describe it like the Netherlands, it's not completely flat. You yourself, Mr. Lukic, may I reminds you, said to me that the Major Sljivancanin took Mr. Vance to the top of a hill, gave him binoculars to look at the town so your statement now that it was completely flat, I'm afraid is incorrect and inconsistent with what Major Sljivancanin told you and what you said yesterday in court was inaccurate and incorrect. So when I answer your question, I have to say the truth, what happened. The hotel was pointed -- excuse me, not the hotel, excuse me. The hospital was pointed out to us and the bridge across that little stream which is -- I learned now is called the -- I believe Vuka River but it's a stream, really. It's very small. Was also indicated to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree that it was indicated to you. My position, however, and the position of my client is that this was pointed out to you from the only elevation in the town called Milovo Brdo. An exceptional feature of this moment was the fact that Mr. Vance used binoculars to get a better view from there. Now, this is my position. Can you please describe that rifle for us, what size, what calibre, what type, what make?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot, Mr. Lukic. And you know that. One would have to be an armaments expert to describe the calibre, the type, the registration number. It was a long weapon. May have been a rifle. It could have been a shotgun gun, although I doubt it since it was a military weapon. I would suspect that it was probably a semi-automatic, long weapon. Either a Uzi or an AK47, something like that probably, standard issue in the JNA, but I think probably Major Sljivancanin is a better person to answer that question than I. I can only report what I saw, namely that a long weapon was elevated and pointed at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 62 of your diary, you have it in front of you, you describe the view while ago on your way to the hospital, you're quite decided about this. You can't see the centre of town but you can see most of the town anyway. Did you go, did you proceed to go to the centre after you recorded this?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We drove all around, we drove all around the city, as you know -- please let me finish my answer. As you know, Vukovar is a city of some 50, 60.000 people, so naturally it had suburbs, it has a centre, it has an area outside the centre. We -- as I noted, much -- we saw much of the city. We may indeed have been at the centre without anybody telling us. That's quite possible. You have to remember, Mr. Lukic, that we were driving around, getting in, getting out of the APC, in a heavily destroyed urban area, and one doesn't write down every street corner one sees. I'm sure you understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm saying this because on the 16th, on page 27 of the transcript, you testified you were describing the spot where this rifle incident took place. We were standing in a square or rather a small square in the middle of the city. That is why I understood that you had at one point reached the centre of Vukovar without necessarily recording the fact in your diary.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've -- you used the word small square where -- which I used -- as I just explained, it was an open area. It was an open area. The sun was shining. That's where the hospital -- that's where he raised the rifle, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The dialogue that we saw in the video a while ago and I have provided you with a transcript so you can have a look, please, if you like, can you please just tell me if you agree with me: We see Mr. Sljivancanin utter some words and there is no reference to the bridges being mined or indeed damaged. There is very clear reference to the existence of minefields between us, as it were, Operations Group South and Operations Group North on the other hand. It was based on that dialogue that I drew the following conclusion. I'm not sure if you agree. This stream, as you called it, the Vuka, was the boundary between the two operations groups. Was that your impression? Because my conclusion is based on the fact that we see Mr. Vance saying, "Can we then please get in touch with someone from Operations Group North" when expressing his desire to go to the hospital. Did you know at the time that there was a distinction between the two operations groups and that Mr. Sljivancanin was talking about mine obstacles? These are two questions, in fact.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not know of the distinction until it was made during the violent altercation between Major Sljivancanin and Mr. Vance. We had been told, and I so noted in my diary, at the Negoslavci briefing, that the briefer, who it turns out to be Colonel Mrksic, was the commander of the southern front. That -- he was introduced that way, in a normal procedure. That was the last that I recall of north versus south. Indeed, why would we be receiving the briefing from the commander of the southern front if he wasn't the commander of the entire situation, you see. I mean if, for example, there was a jurisdictional dispute within the JNA, as to who had control, we would expected the commander of the northern front to brief Mr. Vance. That is to say, if there was a commander. So we -- Colonel Mrksic was introduced and it was not an issue. He briefed us, we proceeded to the city. The first we heard of this -- what you refer to as the northern command was during the violent altercation between Major Sljivancanin and Mr. Vance, when he stated, that is the major stated, that he could not take Mr. Vance, he could not permit us to visit the hospital because it lay in the area of the northern command. We understood that to be a phoney excuse because we had already heard and were hearing several other phoney untruths from Major Sljivancanin, mines, bridges, there was one after another and that is why you could see on Mr. Vance's face this very distraught look, and when the phrase "northern command" was mentioned - I believe it's in the transcript - Mr. Vance says, and we read in the transcript, "Well, take us to the northern command." In other words, he was trying to do everything he could to get to see the hospital, which obviously he was prevented from being allowed to do. One pretext after another was brought forward, and the question of whether Major Sljivancanin said the bridge is mined or the roads are mined or there are mines in front of us, he may have said all three, you see. This was a running conversation, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, in this particular dialogue there is nothing about bridges being mined or damaged, this particular portion that we have just seen.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I recall him saying the bridges were mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please try to draw another conclusion based on the video? If you like, we can play it again, although that might prove a difficult request for my associates. Maybe we can just replay this one moment, please focus on the video, not on the transcript. Based on the footage that we are about to show you, can you see that Mr. Vance is talking to anyone else or is he only talking to Mr. Sljivancanin and nobody else?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were asked yesterday whether Mr. Vance or indeed anyone else from your delegation regarding their desire to visit the Vukovar Hospital, whether they spoke to anyone else during this entire visit, because now we are going to try and find out who else was there, you said that all your requests were being directed to one person, your host, Mr. Sljivancanin. Does this video perhaps remind you that Mr. Vance or you spoke to someone else about this desire to go and visit the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My recollection is that Major Sljivancanin, as escort officer, was the primary person that Mr. Vance spoke to, but you can hear him say in the video, "I need to talk to my colleagues, I need to consult with my colleagues." He would probably have come back to me, you see, I'm standing somewhere behind him and then he says, "Let's go downtown." There were people around us. There were many press, you can see, the video; indeed, we would not have the video unless there had been press. So there were people around. Now, somebody may have asked Mr. Vance a question as we got back in to the armoured personnel carriers. That's conceivable. You know the way journalists are, they shout questions out at you. But the specific answer to your specific question is that we were under the control, in the hands, of Major Sljivancanin and he was the principal interlocutor, the principal person with whom Mr. Vance discussed this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now we will stay on the same topic and I would like to see the second video footage, which is quite brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this comes from the same report, only five minutes later, and it shows a brief dialogue or, rather, a monologue of Mr. Sljivancanin addressed to Mr. Vance. I was unable to give you the translation in advance to the interpreters, but I did give them the transcript in B/C/S, and I hope they will be able to help us with this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "The forces who were there and surrendered and escaped and have already been evacuated from Vukovar. We did give you a vehicle and everything you need and then you can go there and we'll show you where the hospital is."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can play it again because we didn't hear the last part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear the audio feed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will return to this footage after the break. It's a very brief recording and we will take a look at it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, I heard you say just now that there were journalists following you throughout this visit. Do you remember that? Do you remember that the journalists, and a lot of crews, TV crews, accompanied you during this visit?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They accompanied us again during, I repeat, during the visit, yes. They came and went, I'm sure. I don't think we had the undivided attention of the crews. That would be natural. I have no way of judging. You'd have to ask them whether they were with us the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, in your diary, in two places, you mentioned journalists. First, in Sid, as you visited that place, you stated that there was a large number of Yugoslav journalists present there, and I think you said something to the effect that the JNA would use it to their advantage for their propaganda purposes. And then, as you were describing your visit to Velepromet, you wrote verbatim "many foreign journalists present." So this is something that you noticed and I'm now reminding you that in two places in your diary you recorded that there were many journalists accompanying you during your visit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's in the diary. I've already reported to the Court. There is no dispute about that. There were many press of the printed press, we've seen the video so clearly there were video teams there, and there were both Belgrade journalists and foreign journalists, as I noted in my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, by using the wonders of new technology that are available to us in the courtroom, we are going to play for you a video, and I would like to ask you whether you remember this person, this individual, and here I'm referring to the person to the right of Mr. Vance, wearing a hat. So we are not interested in Mr. Vance or in Mr. Sljivancanin but in this third person. We are going to try to zoom in now. We have three, a total of three frames, and we are going to show all three to you to see if it can be discerned in any of them. Could we see the second frame now, please? I have in mind gentleman who can be seen just below this microphone which occupies a large portion of the photograph. Can we enlarge it a bit more?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. Thank you. I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we have yet another frame, freeze frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm now referring to the person completely to the right, perhaps this is the best shot. Do you remember this person?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not. That is to say do I remember him, I see him in the picture so I'm sure he was standing there but he played -- Mr. Vance was talking to Major Sljivancanin, as is clear from the pictures. I don't know who that person was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Are you the person wearing the blue UN cap?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person wearing the blue UN cap is Colonel Purola, that's H-e-i-k-k-i P-u-r-o-l-a. It's a Finnish name, Heikki -- Colonel Heikki Purola. He was our military adviser on the team and at that time he was the senior military adviser to the Secretary-General of the United Nations. The Secretary-General loaned us Colonel Purola for several of our missions because, as we've discussed extensively, the principal purpose of our mission was to see whether the conditions for UN peacekeeping operation could be established, to discuss the peacekeeping force, to secure the agreement of the parties concerned. And Colonel Purola, being an expert in these matters, naturally accompanied us on the peacekeeping side. So that is Colonel Purola.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to tell you the identity of the man that I inquired about. If I mention his name, perhaps it might refresh your memory. This is Colonel Nebojsa Pavkovic, who at the time had been sent by the office of the federal secretary for National Defence, Mr. Kadijevic, to follow the events in Vukovar. So this is Nebojsa Pavkovic. Does this name mean anything to you in relation to the events of that day, not later on?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it means nothing in -- either in regard to events of the day or to any subsequent event.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't need this frame any longer. Yesterday you said that accompanying you from Belgrade were the JNA officers, who had been sent by the organisers of your visit. I'm going to put a simple question to you. Perhaps it's of a theoretical nature and I hope the Prosecutor won't mind me putting this question. You did say that you were an adviser to NATO. So tell me this: Can a major refuse to comply with the orders issued to him by a colonel who is his immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just give us typical examples.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In normal military practice senior officers give the orders to those beneath them. That's quite common, as you say, in a theoretical fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have another theoretical question. Somebody who is in charge of a certain area, area of his responsibility, can he move into somebody else's area of responsibility and bring with him people, visitors, without receiving a permission of the person in command of that area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But he needs the permission presumably of the person in charge of that area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two points, Mr. Lukic, in answer to your contention. First, he wouldn't really, because situations on the ground determine realities. No army would ever win a battle if it stuck irrevocably to its battle plan arranged before the battle occurred. Second point, Mr. Vance had made it known well before the trip that the purpose of the mission was to visit Vukovar that day, and he had specifically mentioned the hospital. So it was known to those who arranged the trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in that group of officers accompanying you from Belgrade, there was also a colonel in charge of security of Mr. Kadijevic, federal secretary of defence? MR. LUKIC [Interpretation] The Prosecutor will know that this man was Mr. Sljivancanin's direct superior in the area of security matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the name Dragoljub Djukic mean anything to you, or perhaps the person who occupied that post for security matters? Was there a Colonel Djukic accompanying you from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name means nothing to me. He might have been there. As I noted in my diary, we went in a JNA motorcade. There were several vehicles. It was a motorcade. So he could well have been in one of them. Mr. Vance and I were in an armoured personnel carrier, which, as we all know, has very limited space.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to mention another name, and perhaps it will be of assistance if I tell you that he was a colonel who, at the time, was head of the liaison office for liaising with foreign visitors and so on. This person frequently attended the meetings between you and Mr. Kadijevic and it might also be helpful if I told you that he spoke excellent English and frequently served as an interpreter. His name is Colonel Petar Stojic. He frequently also interpreted.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that -- he's not a really familiar person or name to me. One doesn't normally ask interpreters their names. I'm sure he was a very good interpreter or General Kadijevic would not have made use of his services. But the name is not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see him in some parts of the footage but -- not as he's interpreting but, rather, coming in and out of various shots. And he will be able to confirm this when he comes here to testify. If I were to tell you that this person wrote down the schedule for the visit of Mr. Vance, he did it personally, and if I were to tell you next that he claims that the visit of the hospital in Vukovar was not discussed back in Belgrade but, rather, only emerged once you arrived in Vukovar, what would you say to this?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that he's not correct, that it was widely known, and it's made clear in the diaries, how concerned Mr. Vance was about the hospital. He has his opinion. He's entitled to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you say that, let us go back to your diary. The first time I see the hospital mentioned in your diary on that day was during your visit to the small hospital, as you called it. You say, "CRV's request to visit the main hospital has been refused." This is the first and only time that you record in the diary this reason for visiting Vukovar, which you deem to be very important. Am I right in claiming this?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said previously, the diary journals are not a stenographic record of everything seen or heard by me after October 1991; what you have said in the diary, what you've read from the diary is true. The fact remains that the principal purpose of the visit, as is recorded in the diaries by what we were told, was to visit the hospital. Now, whether Mr. Vance mentioned that at point A or point B or point C or point X or point Y, it was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have mentioned all of these things several times already, and your position is quite clear. Let me just remind you of what you said and what was recorded in line 19. You said "It's made clear in the diaries how concerned Mr. Vance was about the hospital." All I say is that the hospital is mentioned only once in your diary and at the end of your visit. Is that right? That was all I asked. It's a very clear question.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'll give you a very clear answer. The reason we have pursued this, and, as you've said, I've made the point several times, is that I've been asked the question several times, Mr. Lukic. So let's be clear on that point. I trust we are clear on that point. Now, you asked the question again and I answer again, the diary is correct. It says what it says. It's in front of you. It's in front of me. I read, "Vance's request to visit main hospital rejected." "Weak excuse by JNA." JNA here is synonymous with meaning Sljivancanin. Period. "Scene ensues," that is the violent -- that is -- that summarises the climax of the obstruction -- of the obstructive efforts to keep Mr. Vance away from the hospital. That is the answer. Now, if you want to go over that question again, I'm happy to read it to you. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us that you could understand our language a little bit based on your knowledge of Russian. Did Mr. Vance perhaps speak our language? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that Colonel Stojic personally, and not my client, decided, since he was in charge of scheduling your visit and we will hear this later on from him, so it was Colonel Stojic who decided that it wasn't safe to go to the hospital, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say to that that our interlocutor was Major Sljivancanin. What you say is your contention, your allegation, your assertion. It may be accurate. It may not be accurate. But I cannot judge that because I did not know that at the time. Indeed I'm hearing it now for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why I asked you whether you and Mr. Vance spoke Serbian. I just wanted to establish whether you were able to hear that personally, directly. We will hear from other witnesses about this later on. Mr. Okun, you will agree with me, won't you, that you were not the only person - you and Mr. Vance - visiting Vukovar at the time. There were many other people accompanying you, both members of your delegation and journalists?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Our team was a small one. There were numerous journalists. How many, I could not say. But certainly, you know, I would say half a dozen at the minimum. I can't give you any more accurate figures but there were -- yes, there was certainly more than Mr. Vance and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that during that time, during the Vukovar operation, public opinion, and by this I have in mind international media outlets, closely followed the events in Vukovar and that they didn't really favour the JNA in their reports, they didn't really have a favourable opinion of it. I think that you followed media reports quite closely. I think you said that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've said before - as you again repeat the question, I'm happy to answer it - the events in and around Vukovar were widely reported in the press. You say accurately that the bulk of the western press was critical of the Serb position, and therefore of the JNA. That is also accurate. We did not rely on press reports alone, although naturally we read the daily newspaper. Most people in the world do that. You may even read a newspaper yourself, Mr. Lukic. That is why we were there to find out the facts for ourselves, and that is why, as you see in the diaries, we had meeting after meeting after meeting with Milosevic, with the prime minister, Markovic, with General Kadijevic, with admiral Brovet, precisely to ascertain the real situation, not just that being reported in the foreign press. And, of course, we, as is normal, would receive summaries of the Yugoslav press, of the Belgrade press. So we did our best to keep ourselves informed of public opinion, of journalistic opinion, but above all we relied on what we saw with our own eyes and what was told to us by other parties and we compared notes and reported this back to the Security Council. And as I've mentioned, and I think it's worth mentioning again, our reports are public documents and they were made at the time. So you can see quite clearly what Mr. Vance's and my views were, and we so reported our views to the Security Council on a timely basis through the good offices of the Secretary-General of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The break is near. You're asking me not to interrupt you. I fully respect your approach, your effort to fully clarify certain things. However, this is a question and answer session, and at the outset you provided very clear answer to my question. But that was only the initial part. I wanted to know about the international media and the way they treated the JNA. I have no doubt about your intention to get timely information on all these aspects. You gave me a clear answer. You said that there was a critical approach by most of the world's media and that was my reading of your answer. I'm talking about influential international media monitoring the Yugoslav crisis and particularly the military operations involved. So, please, if you can answer me yes or no, what about influential international media? Were they more inclined not to favour JNA and were they, rather, critical of JNA operations?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were critical.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it maybe now time to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. We will break now and resume at half past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You remember what we spoke about before the break, sir. We spoke about the way the media, the international media more specifically, treated the JNA. Do you remember that at the time, on international TV stations, bits of footage were frequently shown, showing what they referred to as Chetnik-type persons, showing persons who did not appear to be members of any regular military unit?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubt they did show people like that. I can't [Realtime transcript read in error, "can"] vouch for what appeared on every television station around the world, but I'm pretty sure they showed that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't believe my colleague from the OTP will call this speculation. Was there anything else you wished to say, sir?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I might correct the -- my answer as it appears on the screen, I said I can't -- that is to say cannot -- vouch for what appeared on every television station and on the screen it says "I can vouch." So I hope that could be corrected. I would be -- it would be quite a feat to be able to say that you can vouch for everything. Thank you. I'm sorry. It's just on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm glad that sometimes witnesses are also able to give us a hand with the transcript. My next question is about your personal status as a Professor of international relations. Therefore, I do not think this constitutes speculation. Would it not be a first-rate sensation throughout the world that an officer of the JNA uses a rifle or a raised tone of voice when speaking to a personality, a well-known person like Cyrus Vance?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might. It might not. There were lots of things happening at this time in Croatia. Osijek was under siege. Dubrovnik was under siege and being shelled. Incidently, the attacks in and around Dubrovnik, at Pakrac and Dubrovnik probably received the most attention. It was the single most reported item across some period. So Mr. Vance's visit was not the only thing going on in Yugoslavia or in Croatia at the time, and, in addition, there were also -- excuse me. And there were also other actors on the stage. The EC, the monitors, Lord Carrington. I don't say that to downplay or in any way underestimate Mr. Vance's importance. I mention it in answer to your question, to indicate that there were many other important events occurring at that time, which were covered by the international press, both in Yugoslavia and in the rest of the world. I might just recall one case, but it makes the point, I think. The Soviet Union, that is to say the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was in the last weeks of its existence. This is a world-historic event, the collapse of the system inside the Soviet Union. I don't think anybody would disagree. And that sort of thing was also being covered in the press. So there were many other things going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now try to remind you perhaps this is something you don't even know. Something that happened on the next day was a lot more benign than what you describe, in terms of the actors on the stage, as well as in terms of facts, the alleged clash between my client and a representative of the International Red Cross - without the rifle, though, there was only an altercation - received a lot of media exposure, and made it into the Prosecutor's opening statement. Do you agree with me when I say that the Vukovar operation, at least in those days when it was drawing to a close was very much in the public eye of the international media? Please say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was to a degree in the public eye. I've already reported to the Court that there were journalists present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it is your opinion that brandishing a rifle, as Mr. Sljivancanin purportedly did, would not have received so much publicity if the rifle was brandished at Mr. Vance? Am I understanding your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a matter for the press to answer. You might wish to call the journalists who were on the scene. All I can report to you, Mr. Lukic, is what I saw that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that I personally, and I've seen a great deal of footage in different videos, as I believe had my friends from the OTP, never saw this incident reported by any of the TV stations. What's more, I never came across any newspaper articles covering this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to the form of this question. This isn't a question. It's a personal opinion expressed by the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Lukic, that is a well-founded point. You might ask the witness whether he's seen any TV coverage showing the matter but unless you come and get in the witness box, which isn't recommended, you shouldn't be giving all of that in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That much is certain, Your Honour. I will comply with your instruction. Maybe my question was a bit too lengthy and it was based far too much on my own observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever come across any newspaper articles in those days covering this incident involving the rifle that was raised at Mr. Vance? Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing it. Of course, I again, as we discussed earlier, I wasn't in Yugoslavia to monitor the television screens. And also, as you can see from the diary, the days were so full of intense activity that it would have been very difficult, actually, to find more than a few moments free. I had very little free time, as you can note from the diaries, and as I tell you today. Have I answered your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know if the American embassy, and you were a citizen of the United States, still are, or anyone from the UN ever filed an official complaint about the fact that one of their representatives was threatened or attacked? Was there a complaint ever filed with the Yugoslav Ministry of Foreign Affairs? I'm not talking about your discussions with Kadijevic but rather about official relations between two states.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Did the United Nations file a formal, written complaint" is your question. My answer is not to the best of my knowledge. I repeat again that we reported the overall situation regularly to the Security Council, and you can find the general picture expressed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, in all these trials, reports to the UN are a matter of judicial notice. Therefore, I don't believe that I should comment on this any further or tender any of those into evidence but this is something that I verified yesterday and I believe we shall have an opportunity to tender these documents and show them to the Trial Chamber even if your absence. Sir, you said that some of your information was also based on the printed media. The footage that we saw yesterday is from TV Belgrade. We May assume a certain amount of bias in relation to the JNA on their part, I think. Would I be right in saying that at the time, as were you watching the news, TV news, you would have been more inclined to believe such stations as CNN or TV France as opposed to TV Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You would not be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That probably means that I am mistaken on this point. Why would you think that the RTS for example was more objective in its coverage of the Vukovar front than the BBC? Just to name one example.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really think that my speculating about the journalistic ethics and morals of one television station against another is particularly relevant to what I saw with my own eyes in Vukovar on November 19th, 1991, between 11 a.m. and 1 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You probably realise that what I've been trying to do is to challenge what you say you witnessed, and that's why I'm asking all these questions.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Q. I would like to ask that another video of this same visit, Mr. Vance's visit, be shown now. This is a BBC video. This is another 65 ter document that we received from the Office of the Prosecutor. This is a very short recording. It lasts about three minutes, even less. What I wish to say now is this is a report in English. It will easy for you to understand. The problem I'm facing at the moment is I don't have a B/C/S transcript of the report for which I would like to apologise to my clients. In due course we shall have the conversations translated and disclosed to my client. So this is a BBC report. It's in English. It's very brief. Can we please have a look? This is Exhibit 315 from the OTP 65 ter list. It's a video marked as V 0000802-1. Can we please now go ahead and have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "... two parts of this shattered town by the Danube. His hosts were federal army commanders and he went with them in an armoured column no closer to the centre than the inner suburbs, which have also been damaged. But it wasn't all Mr. Vance had come to see. He was here to see if it was possible to set up a peacekeeping force [unintelligible], and today in Vukovar by his presence to help save lives if possible. "Make arrangements for the people in the northern command to see the hospital. "He was told it wasn't possible because it wasn't safe. But he was taken to the reception centre where thousands of refugees, mostly Croats, are taken in after surviving the two-month siege. "'I was living in the basement,' she said, 'a mortar shell fell on the house and I was injured.' "While he was there a bus arrived bringing more people in from the ruins. This is where the survivors find out if their relatives are dead or alive." "Well, I think this is tragic to see the conditions these people have been living under and suffering of them. "And here is what Mr. Vance didn't see, the centre of Vukovar or what remains of it with the federal army firmly in control and some fighting still going on. "Under fire, civilians were still coming out of their cellars. It seems that not all the Croatian soldiers had surrendered. The federal army and Serbian irregulars were dealing with them."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this marked for identification, unless the OTP have any objections. It's their own exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be MFI 72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it can be marked as an exhibit at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will -- in any event that will be Exhibit D72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I make the point, Mr. Lukic, that the earlier video clips that you showed have, as far as I know, not been exhibited, unless they are part of something that is already an exhibit. So you might want to give attention to that before you finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm bearing that in mind, Your Honour. The short clips that we saw, the freeze frames, were taken from the -- some of the materials that have already been tendered. I will probably be dealing with that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe you understood this clip in its entirety, the sound, at least, of this recording. In your opinion, and you were there, do you think this offers an objective view of what was going on in Vukovar on that day. The journalist's name is Martin Bell.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is generally correct, and I'm -- I've never seen it before, incidently. I'm seeing it today for the first time. And I notice he calls the town "shattered," which confirms what I wrote in my diary. He says in there we did not see the downtown. He says that on the video, and I so reported that in my diary. There are pictures at the refugee reception centre, and you'll notice Mr. Vance talking to some of the civilian victims of the siege and I reported that in my diary. So, yes, I think it's consistent. You see the reuniting of the families. I would say it's generally consistent and again we could see -- I could see in the video the awful destruction that had been wrought on Vukovar. The principal impression, Mr. Lukic, I might just add, to give you the full picture of the day and of these films, the principal impression one came away with from Vukovar, the overall impression, the general impression, was of the destruction. That's the sort of thing that was constant. It was with us every moment because we were driving around in an urban city that was virtually destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is new to me in this video is the bit where Mr. Bell is reporting from what he calls the centre, and we can hear sounds of shooting. You did hear that, right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it on the video. I heard no sounds of shooting myself personally during that day. Or I should say I don't recall hearing any sounds of shooting. We got in and got out of the APCs. You could see Mr. Vance getting back into one of our APCs in that BBC picture. Nobody ever said to us, you know, keep your head down, duck, there are bullets flying, there is opposition in the town. No. Nobody ever said that to us. We felt quite secure in the hands of the JNA and of Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is perhaps the key to my position. You were not physically present where the shooting took place, were you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the assumption that there was shooting, we heard sounds of it, we did not see actual scenes of combat on the picture. The sounds we heard could have easily been made by JNA soldiers shooting their rifles into the air to celebrate the fall of Vukovar. I'm not alleging that. I'm not suggesting it. But it could have happened. Because we are talking about sounds, not about combat. Martin Bell said you can hear the sounds and he said there is still some resistance in the city. I would not challenge what he says. But what I'm saying to the Court is that during our entire time in Vukovar, I did not hear sounds of firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you just confirm this, please? You saw the footage that we saw yesterday, and the footage that was shown two days ago, and the BBC footage right now. Did you notice yourself in any one of these clips, any one of the frames shown?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You described the scene in Negoslavci. We saw that. Martin Bell's BBC report, he is covering the visits of Mr. Vance. We don't know if he was there all the time but he did report on the visit. There isn't a single reference to any altercation, raised voices, or arguments, or rifles being raised. There is not a single reference to it. Would that seem to be correct to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. I haven't seen the whole film. I hear you say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you about the bit that we saw. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the video clip, this excerpt from something that you showed us, he does not mention the altercation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you several times about the timing of your visit, the precise schedule, and you gave us information from your diary, and you said that the visit to Vukovar took place between 11 and 1300 hours on that day, following which you went to Belgrade and so on. I'm going to read something to you in the official language. [In English] "Afternoon of 19 of November 1991, JNA units under the command of the Mile Mrksic took control of Vukovar Hospital."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what was the date you gave?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the afternoon of the 19th of November. [Interpretation] Do you know whose claim this is?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just read out to you paragraph 29 from the indictment against Mr. Sljivancanin, namely that the JNA entered the hospital in the afternoon hours on the 19th. This is the case of Mr. Moore and his team.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I understand you to be saying, if I understand you correctly, Mr. Lukic, that the Prosecution says -- maintains that the JNA was in control of the hospital beginning at 12.01 p.m. The afternoon starts at noon. We are not here to count the seconds or the nanoseconds, but afternoon begins at noon. That's what you're saying they said. Yes. I understand that -- what you are saying about what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This timing, and the exact timeline of when the JNA entered the hospital will be discussed here later on, and we will not focus on that now. But to go back to what you told us before the break, and when I asked you about areas of responsibility and what your position is concerning areas of responsibility in wartime, I understood that your position is that these matters are not that significant in formal terms.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said the opposite. I said they are significant formally but that in reality, in action, they may be overridden. Excuse me, sir, but since you ask, I would like to give you the correct answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He was in charge of your security. This is what you said and this is what in large portion is in accordance with my case. What I'm claiming is that during your visit in Vukovar, he was at no time responsible for the safety of the Vukovar Hospital. This is our position. And I hope Mr. Moore is not going to give me the looks he gave me just a little ago. I'm not going to ask you to speculate, but bearing in mind the distinguished status that you have as a diplomat and as a politician, let me ask you this: You mentioned the US constitution, the army, and similar issues and I will put you a simple question. If a delegation came to the US, same level as your delegation that visited Vukovar, and if one of your people learned that there were enemies within that group, say members of al Qaeda, would they have allowed you to go into a building without first checking whether the building was safe?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do object. I don't look in any way. It's just pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the ambassador can cope with that sort of speculation, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would answer to that, and I must say that it is only speculation -- I'm not a politician, by the way, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's nice of to you give me that honour but I'm a working diplomat, or I was. I've described Major Sljivancanin as we saw him that day, you know. He didn't come with a curriculum vitae, and give us anything like that. I've already told you in answer to your questions that I wasn't aware of the other colonels who you say were on the scene. I don't deny it. I just wasn't aware of them because as I have said in response to your repeated questions, Major Sljivancanin was the escort officer. He was the man you can see in all the film that you've shown talking with Mr. Vance so that is why we remember Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the reply to my question? Would you have banned the entrance into the building?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you ask a speculative question. We can spend a lot of time speculating on this or that building. I really don't know. It's pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge thought that you would be able to answer the question but if not, I'm not going to insist on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I let the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I have answered the question, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. Thank you. I have, Mr. Lukic, let you go with that question, but don't try and make more of the concession I gave you than should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies if you believe that I wanted to abuse the situation, but I believed that a person of the reputation and of the experience as this witness would be able to give me an answer. But I can see that he's a true diplomat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another question that has to do with the factual situation: These Chetnik-type individuals that you mentioned in your diary as being in the collection centre or refugee centre, did they seem to welcome you there, these people?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They neither welcomed us, nor attacked us in any way. They were lounging around. They were, as I've described, many rough -- I quote, "Many rough customers, armed irregulars, et al." They didn't interfere with us. They didn't facilitate our visit. They were there, just mingled with the JNA troops. It was, you know, it was daytime. They were smoking, almost all of them were smoking, rough chaps with -- unshaven types, slovenly uniforms, but in something like a uniform but they did not welcome or disabuse -- or abuse our presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday on page 34 of the transcript, when answering the question of Mrs. Tapuskovic, you uttered something that seemed interesting to me. When she asked you about the mines placed around the barracks in Croatia, you said that you personally didn't go and check that because otherwise you would have been blown up had you entered the minefield. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did not check on every occasion a minefield. We did on certain occasions check. I can give you examples to answer your question. About a week or so later, en route to visit the besieged city of Osijek, which I mentioned previously, we were taken through the mines. We were handed over from the JNA to the Croatian army, and at one point during that visit, the road that we travelled on, which we assumed was safe, again we were travelling in -- on that occasion in an ECMM vehicle. We travelled in a vehicle driven by the European monitors, but we were under the control of the JNA and later when they handed us to the Croatians, and in fact the road that we were travelling on had been mined. Somebody mined it to blow us up because there was a thin wire stretched across the road, and fortunately the driver of our car spotted it before. So -- and we went out and we -- they showed us the mines on either side of the road. That's in my diary. You can check it. So that was one occasion whether we checked on mines personally. The other -- second occasion, and I'll only mention this, is that we had to assume that there were mines around the Tito caserne in Zagreb because it was being blockaded and we went into the caserne the next day, in fact - that's in my diary; we could discuss that - for the lengthy meeting and very useful meeting that we had with General Raseta. So you know, the issue of mines was, I suppose, all around. Croatia was a battlefield in many areas. And those were just two of our personal experiences. Again, I say since we were taken in to the barracks by the Croatians in Zagreb, they probably knew where their mines were. They must have laid them themselves or been aware of it. They were controlling the situation inside -- in and around the Tito caserne. So we were probably led through the -- some mines. But I can't vouch for it. I didn't, you know, go around with a mine detector sweeping the ground, sniffing dogs or something. That really wasn't my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My next question has to do precisely with this topic that I just raised. It might be helpful if you turn to page 93 of your diary, which records the conversation with Kadijevic. Do you know that that evening, after you went to Belgrade, in the immediate vicinity of the Vukovar Hospital, three soldiers were killed by a mine, their bodies charred? There are many reports describing this. This happened en route between the bridge and the hospital. I directed you to your diary because you record there that Mr. Kadijevic informed you about the death of two soldiers. He said two. Do you have any other details regarding this?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. What's in the diary would be the relevant comment on your question. I note on page 93 that you refer to, I thank you for refreshing my memory, that Mr. Vance interrupted General Kadijevic, most unusual, most unusual for Mr. Vance, and it shows the emotion that he felt even two days after the incident at Vukovar. Two days after he still felt so strongly about the obstructionism and the lies he had been told n his opinion, by the JNA and specifically by Major Sljivancanin, but he interrupted General Kadijevic and described the obstruction of his Vukovar visit briefly but strongly. That's a quote. Vance describes obstruction of his Vukovar visit briefly but strongly. So I think that indicates pretty clearly that Vance even two days later was very angry about the treatment he had received at the hands of Major Sljivancanin and the JNA in Vukovar on November 19, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I must say, Mr. Okun, that I have a hard time dealing with my questions and your answers. My question was very simple. Did you hear that on that road leading to the hospital, three soldiers were killed that night? Did you hear that or not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard that from General Kadijevic. That we heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. [Interpretation] In your testimony, you frequently said that my client had lied to you in describing the barracks, the number of shells that handed, the bridges and so on. What you observed during the four hours of your visit --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two hours, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Two hours of visiting Vukovar and the vicinity. My client, as the security officer who had been there in the preceding two months, had better information than you did about the safety and security in the area. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I hear you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that is your reply?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of your assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My client and you agree on one issue. Perhaps even more, but one seems relevant. As we were watching the video clip, he said, and as did you, that the United States and Yugoslavia fought on the same side during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That is a fact. Well, to be accurate in truth, we fought on the same side with those, Marshal Tito and others, who fought against Nazi Germany. So in that respect, we were also fighting against the occupied territory of Yugoslavia, but broadly speaking we certainly fought with the anti-Nazi forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because of something that has to do with your departure from Vukovar. My client says, and you can tell me if he's mistaken, that Mr. Vance and he shook hands and that on that occasion Mr. Vance said something like this: "Major, I can see that you're fond of history. If you ever do write about these events, then please write the truth. This is just one battle." Do you remember that this is how Mr. Vance and my client parted?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it specifically, Mr. Lukic, but what you say is broadly consistent with the behaviour of Cyrus Vance. He is a very senior, a very practised man, and a very polite person. He's a very courteous individual, so that he shakes somebody's hand is clear. I'm interested to hear that you say that Mr. Vance said to Major Sljivancanin, upon departure, if I understood you correctly, you quoted Mr. Vance as saying something like, "If you ever write about this, please tell the truth." And that, which I thank you for refreshing my memory again, is consistent with Mr. Vance because he believed that Major Sljivancanin had not told him the truth in Vukovar. That is precisely why he said to the major, "if you write about it, please tell the truth," meaning do not behave, do not talk, the way you've talked to me, because you have not told me the truth. And I think that's a pretty obvious conclusion that one can draw from that, because it would not necessarily be the kind of thing that you would expect a mediator to say to his escort officer, "Please tell the truth." I mean, he would say that if he believed he had not heard the truth and that, of course, is what Mr. Vance believed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You never once heard, nor did I personally say to anyone there in Vukovar - I'm not referring to your meeting with Kadijevic later - that the information you were receiving was not true. Did you ever say to Sljivancanin that what you were hearing there was not true, you or Mr. Vance?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vance made clear by his actions as well as his words that he disbelieved Major Sljivancanin. I've told you and I need not repeat, that they had a shouting match, that their voices were very loud, that in all my years with Mr. Vance I had never seen him so angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You and Mr. Vance went to see Mr. Kadijevic. You told us the details that you remembered about that visit. You told us that again. Do you remember that on that occasion, Mr. Vance received a gift from Mr. Kadijevic, namely a pistol?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall our -- I don't recall his receiving a pistol but it's quite conceivable that he did. He and General Kadijevic had good personal relations. They respected each other. Indeed, on a subsequent mission, after General Kadijevic retired - he was replaced by General Adzic - it was learned that he had cancer, and he was hospitalised. The cancer was very serious. He was not expected to survive. Mr. Vance and I visited him in the hospital a few days before his death. That serves again to give you an example of Cyrus Vance, how he acts, how he behaves, his respect for people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose that before you entered the courtroom the Prosecution showed you the video clips that we saw here during the trial. You just told us that you never saw this BBC clip before. I supposed that the Prosecution showed you the video material that they have.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was shown by the Prosecution, the video material, was the drive-in to the city, the first item that was shown, and the exchange between the major and Mr. Vance, the one about which we have the transcript. I did not see the BBC picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is one of my final questions. In any one of these video clips that you saw, can my client be seen with a rifle?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I saw. I did notice him wearing his side arm in one of the video clips, but he did not normally carry a rifle. That's partially one of the reasons why it seemed so unusual at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, I'm about to conclude my cross-examination but I have one final question, which is a result, as it were, of the questions that I've asked so far. You said that your visit to Vukovar was followed by a group of journalists from a number of different media. You were being escorted by a number of different persons, JNA officers, perhaps you can't confirm this because you don't know their names but you were surrounded by people throughout. How do you explain the fact that you seem to have been the only person to see my client with a rifle? This was never once pointed out in any of the reports or mentioned anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well the answer to that, Mr. Lukic, is I would say really quite clear. There were people, they came and went from time to time. We've established that. I did not say that Major Sljivancanin -- I've never said and it isn't true that he raised -- elevated the rifle to his eye like a marksman. What I've said is that he brandished this long weapon, and it was a very quick gesture, no more than a couple of seconds, but brandish the weapon he did, and it may have been just in a moment of high emotion on his part. You can ask him that yourself. I'm sure you will. He may have been a bit out of himself because it was a long day, he had been discussing the visit and the visit to the hospital with increasing ferocity with Mr. Vance. We've covered that thoroughly. We went from a discussion to a debate, they went from a debate to an argument. They went from an argument to an altercation. They went from a verbal altercation to a shouting match. I've reported that several times. So this may have been the major just being overcome by emotion and he may have wanted to just to indicate by the rifle, you know, let's end this thing. Now, I've also said and reported to the Court in answer to a previous question, that neither I nor Mr. Vance expected him to shoot. I didn't think he was going to shoot me at any time and I'm quite certain that Mr. Vance didn't think he was going to shoot him. But raise the rifle he did. And to be very specific on your question of why you say nobody else reported this, again, I can only say we were dealing and the journalists, of course, all of them, have been dealing with this situation of widespread violence, you know, thousands of people had died. We were travelling in a shattered city, utterly destroyed, cities were still under siege. That was the reality of Croatia at that time. I'm only describing the reality of what we saw. We can obviously people argue about who did what to whom but that's what people were aware of, is the -- was the violence. Indeed we reported on that. That was one of our jobs in establishing the peacekeeping operation. I've just jotted down, if I may, two sentences, to read to you from a report we made -- the Secretary-General's report of December 11, the first report after this incident. It's his report to the Security Council on the cease-fire and on peacekeeping. Two sentences. I quote, "It is the view of my personal envoy --" that's Mr. Vance. "It is the view of my personal envoy that all sides, and especially the irregular forces, have been wanting in observing the Geneva Agreement in respect of the cease-fire. It also appears to be the case that the cease-fire violations by JNA have been more numerous and certainly more violent." That is in UN document S/23280, I repeat, S/23280, dated 11 December 1991, in section 1, page 7. You can find it easily. It will take you a minute. I found it, and I'm not very good on the Internet, but I found it on the Internet last night. That was what was going on, violence everywhere. And the most violence, as Mr. Vance reported, was being perpetrated by the JNA. That was reported at the time. We don't have to rely on memory 14 years later. That's what we said what we saw at the time. That's what was reported to the Security Council. I don't need to read it again. I can, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me conclude. We have not seen a single report, a single video, or a piece of TV coverage, no official report, no unambiguous description of the event in your diary, yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me to confirm whether you have seen something. I don't know that I can confirm what you have seen. I can tell you what I have seen. I have not seen it, yes. I have not seen this incident on television, nor have I seen lots of other incidents on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've finished with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Moore, would you expect to be long in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would anticipate I will be 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we might manage to do that 15 minutes now, Mr. Moore, by the look of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That would enable the witness to finish before we break for lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Ambassador, you've been asked many questions, having been shown videos and you've been told about various other officers, a Colonel Djukic, a Colonel Stojic. When Mr. Vance asked to go to see about the bridge, to see about the hospital, and was told, as we can see in the transcript where he says, "Well, maybe somebody else can," after being refused, did you see Major Sljivancanin speak to any other officer present, to ask for permission, clarification, or whether it was possible?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw him speaking to any other officers, although it's possible he did out of my eyesight but at that time it was a dialogue, an increasingly unpleasant dialogue, between Mr. Vance and the major. That is to say during the entire visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal specifically with the video that we have seen at the very start. Have you got the transcript there?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I wonder if we can just play the video. I'm referring specifically to the video that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we fast-forward this, I wonder, to the next part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This should be on page 47256 of the transcript. Do you have that, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it, I think, correctly on 04247244.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is correct. That's the start but if one turns over for 7245 this is actually the part that one is coming to --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- in relation to the northern command to see the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the remark of the major that the JNA originates from the army that fought fascism in the Second World War, that we just heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. If you can just go to 7245, please?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And quite a good reference point is where we heard the words "northern command."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we can play that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, there is the reference. Have you got the point?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Which is number 14, well, maybe somebody else can. Vance speaking to Sljivancanin. Did Sljivancanin refer to any other person when he gave that indication to Vance?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. You have been asked about a man, small man as being described, his name is Pavkovic, the Defence showed you the video. Did you see him play any part in the decision-making process at that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
