utterances.text: Thank you. May we now move on to the cross-examination in relation to the Badinter Commission? You've been asked various questions about that, the various opinions that were requested and subsequently arrived at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, to assist the Court, overnight we have obtained hard copies in relation to opinion 1 that was cross-examined on. Perhaps if that could just be given out at this time and it should also, I hope, appear on the electronic version. The number is O117/1654. And if a copy can be given to the ambassador, please. There should be copies, I hope, for the Court. Copies, I hope, for the Court. That is opinion number 1. And then there are hard copies now for also what is called opinion number 11. I'd ask for copies to be given out in relation to that, please, because it will help the sequence of questions and understanding, I hope. Again, copies are available. That number is 00359856. I attempt to do this in, I hope, a fairly direct way so that we don't waste too much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we now turn, please, to opinion number 1. Do you have that, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it's on the electronic screen. It refers to Lord Carrington, November the 20th, 1991. Can we just deal with the first question and then perhaps we can go through the document as a whole, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The frontispiece, please, thank you very much. "We find ourselves with a major legal question. Serbia considers that those republics which have declared or would declare themselves independent or sovereign have seceded or would secede from the SFRY which would otherwise continue to exist." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. "Other republics on the contrary consider that there is no question of secession but the question is one of a disintegration or breaking up of the SFRY as the result of the concurring will of a number of republics. They consider that the six republics are to be considered equal successors to the SFRY without any of them or group of them being able to claim to be the continuation thereof." And then basically we have the question posed by Carrington. "I should like the arbitration committee to consider the matter in order to formulate any opinion or recommendation which it might deem useful." Now, can we move, then, on, please, to the next page, 655? It basically outlines various criteria, and then going on to 1656, and these are the notes. It's number 2. "The arbitration committee notes that ..." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. "A, although the SFRY has until now retained its international personality, notably inside international organisations, the republics have expressed their desire for independence." I'm not going to deal with the other republics. I want to deal with number 2, please, where it refers to in Croatia. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "In Croatia, by a referendum held in May 1991, followed by a declaration of independence on June 25th, 1991, which was suspended for three months and confirmed on October the 5th, 1991." Now my final part of what may be a lengthy question but just to help all parties, if you turn the page, please, to 71657, where it gives the opinion of the arbitration committee. May I read it? "Consequently, the arbitration committee is of the opinion, A, that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is in the process of dissolution; 2, that is incumbent upon the republics to settle such problems of state secession as may arise from this process in keeping with the principles and rules of international law, with particular regard for human rights and the rights of peoples and minorities." And then it goes on basically saying working together. You were asked about opinion number 1. Now, would you be kind enough, please, to look at the second document, opinion number 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My learned friends should have a B/C/S version as well as the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The date, if we go to page 359858 appears to be Paris, the 16th of July 1993. Have you got that, ambassador, the very -- the page again is 9858, the very end of the English document.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I deal with one or two parts, please? What exactly was the function of the arbitration commission, as you understood it at that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we were told by Lord Carrington, by other people from the EC conference, and by Judge Badinter himself, the purpose of the arbitration commission was to settle the legal and constitutional questions concerning the break-up of Yugoslavia. These were disputed points and so the EC felt it important to have this very distinguished body adjudicate legal and constitutional matters. That was our understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we go to page 98 -- sorry, 9857, please? Again I try and deal with it in relatively precise terms. If we look at paragraph 3, but the second paragraph, which is a short paragraph, it's actually a one-sentence paragraph, reading, "As the commission indicated in opinion number 1," do you have that, ambassador? It's page 9857. Page 9857, "As the commission indicated --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you it should be on the lek version as well. "This is a question of fact. That is to be assessed in each case in the light of the circumstances in which each of the states concerned was created." If we deal, then, with paragraph 4, dealing just with republic, the republics of Croatia and Slovenia, "The issue is the same as regards the republics of Croatia and Slovenia, both of which declared their independence on the 25th of June 1991 and suspended their declarations of independence for three months on the 7th of July 1991, as provided by the Brioni declaration, in accordance with the declaration the suspension ceased to have effect on the 8th of October 1991. Only then did these two republics definitively break all links with the organs of the SFRY and become sovereign states in international law. For then, then, the 8th of October 1991, is the date of the state secession." Now, could you turn the page, please, to 9858, the final page in the hard copy. It's paragraph 10. It should be highlighted, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we were hoping to have it highlighted but we use Sanction as opposed to electronic version, and hard copy, but we'll deal with it in any event. Can we deal with paragraph 10, please. There we are. "The arbitration commission consequently takes the view that the dates upon which the states stemming from the SFRY succeeded to the SFRY are 8th of October 1991 n the case of the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Slovenia," and then recites other dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you were cross-examined in relation to the arbitration commission, are these the documents that you were referring to or not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the conclusions that you find in these documents, do they change the conclusions that you gave in your evidence without the documents?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe they are identical because you may remember I was repeatedly asked on a theoretical basis, abstract questions about control of territory and that sort of thing, stable population, and I said in response to Madam Tapuskovic, that these were matters this were decided on individual merits, and you see that in the arbitration commission's report here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then thirdly, and finally, my question, I hope, is you've been asked by Mr. Lukic repeatedly about the allegation that you have made about the gun being turned on yourself and Mr. Vance. How significant an incident was that to you at the time when, as you say, Sljivancanin lifted a long firearm towards yourself and Vance?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we thought it was important. I've already reported to the court that neither Mr. Vance nor I expected him to shoot us. It was perhaps, again, his purpose, I don't know, but perhaps it was his purpose to say, "It's over, Mr. Vance," you know, "this is the end, no more conversation. You're not going to get to see that hospital." And so that's the way we took it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, unless the Court have any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you tendering these documents, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will be tendering those documents. I think there is no objection to that particular course. That being the case, may we deal, then, please, with what I will call opinion number 1, 1171654, in the English version, concluding on 1657.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P73.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the final document is opinion number 11, which is 9856 until 9858 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P74.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ambassador, you'll be pleased to know that that is the end of the evidence, the questioning has concluded, the Chamber is grateful for your attendance and your assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will rise now. We will resume at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.59 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that you have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Agha?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness is a 92 bis witness and pursuant to order of this Court the transcript has been submitted to the Court. Can the transcript be given an exhibit number if the Court would like to deal with it in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P75, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, two issues regarding the testimony of the witness. The first is that sometimes it is the practice of some Trial Chambers for the advocate to read out a brief summary of what was evidence contained in his transcript for the public consumption and so that the Chamber is aware of the essence of the evidence. That summary does not become a part of the evidence because his evidence is in fact the transcript. So I was wondering if the Court would like to deal with this in a similar manner or just move straight to other issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A summary would be useful. Thank you, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: The second issue is Your Honours, is the exhibits which are associated with the transcript of the witness and it is the submission of the Prosecution that perhaps these exhibits could be briefly run through by the witness so that they can have their own exhibit numbers in this particular trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: By way of a background, the witness was chief of the security command of the 5th Air Force Corps of the JNA based in Zagreb until he resigned in the JNA in July 1991. The witness had worked in the JNA security service for about 20 years. After leaving the JNA, the witness joined the Croatian National Guard now referred to as the ZNG, in August of 1991, where he was appointed as Chief of Staff and commander of the ZNG until 21st September 1991. After this time, the Main Staff of the Croatian army was formed with General Anton Tus as Chief of Staff. From 8th of October 1991, the witness has appointed as chief Croatian negotiator with the JNA, reporting directly to President Tudjman. In this position, the main role of the witness was to negotiate the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia. In his capacity of chief negotiator, the witness was directly involved in negotiations surrounding the shelling and evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital with General Raseta that of the JNA, as well as the ECMM. The witness retired from the Croatian army in December 1992, in the rank of a four-star general. Thereafter he served as the adviser to the president of Croatia on national security issues. He is currently in retirement. Now, in his earlier testimony, the witness gave evidence concerning the reporting structure within the security services of the JNA. The witness's evidence was that the JNA operated under a single unified chain of command. However, officers in the security service of the JNA had two parallel chains of command. The first chain of command was to the commander of the unit to which they were attached. However, when they were dealing with professional matters which exclusively concerned security issues, they reported directly to their superior in the security service. With regard to a commission of a war crime, if the security officer became aware of this, and considered that he ought to be engaged, he would use his sources to investigate the matter and then report back to the commander of his unit and, if necessary, up the chain of command to the security service. With regard to mass deaths, these had to be reported right up the chain of command from the bottom to the top. Although the witness was a part of the air forces' security service, the reporting methods were the same for the land forces' security service. And this usually entailed reporting on a daily basis up the chain of command or immediately if the event was of an emergency nature. The witness then in his evidence ran through various documents which were tendered as exhibits in his prior testimony about various JNA reports relating to killings of civilians in villages such as Skabrnja, Nadin, and Bruska, between November 1991 and March 1992. Pertinently, the 1992 report found that the Benkovac police had no material evidence for the finding that the massacre was a result of Ustasha sabotage an and that the case should be reopened. This, according to the witness, was an example of things being manipulated on the ground to forcefully place blame on the Croats in order to justify JNA intervention on the side of the rebel Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Agha please slow down a little for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I apologise. I've been asked to slow down a little. The witness then gave evidence of the JNA actually siding with the rebel Croatian Serbs. In May of 1990 according to the witness, pursuant to the orders of the JNA, weapons of the Croatian Territorial Defence were moved to warehouses under JNA control. The effect of this order was to disarm Croatia. The JNA, however, through its security administration, began secretly arming the Serbs living in Croatia between the autumn of 1990 and spring of 1991 especially in the area of Eastern Slavonia. To carry out this covert arming the cooperation of the JNA commanders was necessary. Croatia, realising that it was defenceless, began purchasing weapons from outside of Yugoslavia and prepared to protect itself from any aggression, through its police which formed the backbone of the ZNG, which was created in May 1991. According to the witness, the ZNG, however, lacked training, arms, and which meant at its inception there were only weapons for about 30 per cent of its men. Whilst the witness was in the security service, it was had headed by Aleksandar Vasiljevic, who initially was in favour of holding Yugoslavia together at all costs but who later followed the line of the Serb leadership that if Yugoslavia could not be retained in its entirety, it had to be retained in an abridged form, a so-called Greater Serbia. According to the evidence of the witness, the initial plan, plan A, was for the JNA, which it did initially through its security service, to arm the Croatian Serbs, who, with the support of the JNA, would overthrow the Croatian leadership and the JNA would take control of Croatia. However, in the second half of 1991, due to the international factor, this plan was modified to the extent that the JNA would only take over Croatia up to the so-called Virovitica-Karlovac-Karlobag line. Later, according to this witness, this plan was again modified to include the JNA, together with the Serb insurgents taking over territory in Croatia which was predominantly occupied by Serbs. Plan C. This was a far-reduced area and the modification, according to the witness, in the plan was brought about by strong Croatian resistance, the lack of manpower of the JNA, and international pressure. The witness then went on to give evidence concerning the takeover of villages in Croatia by the JNA and the Croatian Serbs, pursuant to this plan C. According to the witness, the JNA tactics in taking over villages in Eastern Slavonia and other parts of Croatia was to shell the village with a view to forcing the villagers to flee and then to attack the village. Thereafter, constant pressure was placed on non-Serbs living in the village by the newly installed Serb authorities to leave the area. According to the evidence of the witness, this tactic was most prominently used in central Dalmatia, Eastern Slavonia, and the Ilok region. In particular, according to the witness, the villages of Ilok, Boksic, Gradjanac [phoen], Rakovica, Jovarnik, and Nijemci were all taken over. The village of Saborsko was razed to the ground and many other Croatian homes were destroyed once their inhabitants had fled. The ancient city of Dubrovnik on the coast was also extensively shelled by the JNA, notwithstanding the witness's complaints to both General Raseta of the JNA and the ECMM. Turning now to Vukovar in particular, as chief Croatian negotiator, the witness had many discussions with General Raseta who represented the JNA in respect of the city of Vukovar. These negotiations were very often carried out in the presence of the ECMM who acted as mediators and usually centred around the position of the sick and the wounded at Vukovar Hospital. General Raseta used to seek orders on issues arising from the negotiations from his superiors in Belgrade who included the deputy SSNO, Admiral Brovet, and the Chief of Staff, General Adzic. With regard to Vukovar, when the witness complained to General Raseta about the shelling of Vukovar and the hospital, and requested that it cease, General Raseta consulted General Zivota Panic on at least one occasion, in whose area of responsibility the hospital was located. General Panic told Raseta that he was present at his observation post and that the hospital was not being hit and that the Croatian side was lying. According to the evidence of the witness, he complained daily to Raseta about the shelling of Vukovar and the hospital but the JNA continually denied that the hospital was being shelled. The witness also complained to the ECMM about the shelling of the hospital. However, they were powerless to do anything. Regarding the evacuation of the hospital, negotiations were conducted with General Raseta by Dr. Andrija Hebrang who was the Croatian Minister of Health. On 18th November, an evacuation agreement was entered into between Croatia and the JNA regarding the evacuation of the hospital. Under the agreement, both Croatia and the JNA agreed to recognise the neutrality of the hospital during the evacuation. The JNA, however, according to the witness, did not abide by the term of the agreement. Shortly after the evacuation of the hospital, the witness learned that many of the patients who were supposed to have been evacuated had not reached their destination. The witness protested daily to General Raseta to return the missing patients. General Raseta, however, claimed that he did not know where the missing patients were. The JNA never gave the witness an explanation of what had happened to the missing patients, even when the Croatian Prime Minister wrote to the JNA asking where the balance of the evacuated patients were, there was silence. Now, that in essence is a summary of the evidence which the witness gave under oath in the Milosevic case, of which this Trial Chamber has admitted the transcripts into evidence. Now, Your Honours, turning to the question of those exhibits which were tendered along with the transcript, the Prosecution would like briefly to run through some of those so that they may be exhibited separately in this trial. And the Prosecution submits that in order for this to be done as expeditiously as possible, that the Trial Chamber would take notice that the foundation for most of these exhibits has already been established in the transcripts. So with the claim's leave, I would like to try to move through them as expeditiously as possible.

So it was not sent toward the command structure but, rather, to other professional services within the security service. This was the typical procedure for reporting. When we had to inform the command structures, we wrote documents that were somewhat different and we didn't provide all of the information, such as the source, and the method applied. We simply briefed them on the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So, General, this is an example of a report going up the security administration chain of command?

It was usually accompanied by other documents such as photographs, sketches, objects found or perhaps their photographs. utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA

utterances.text: As is stated here, this is an official note in its old form that was previously used in the JNA security service. These are some -- probably forms that are left -- that were left over and were used by the security officers of the 180th Motorised Brigade. These two officers, Rosic, Simo and Ostjic, Milivoj, say that they informed the 9th Corps in Knin about the event in Skabrnja described in the previous document by an officer of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, according to this document and one of the earlier documents, this event in Skabrnja and Nadin villages was on the 18th and 19th of November 1991 and the alleged crimes were by Serbian volunteers; is that correct?

utterances.text: Based on the description of events in this official note given by authorised officials, yes. It seems correct, namely that this was done by the volunteers from Serbia and members of the Opacic group which comprised people residing in that area around Skabrnja, Benkovac, and Nadin. The security organs state this and inform their superior within the security service about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So taking these last few exhibits, would it indicate that the JNA command were kept well informed of the events that were happening on the ground, vis-a-vis crimes committed by the Serb volunteers against the Croatian civilian population?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Clearly, based on my assessment and also based on the later analysis of such cases, this seems to be an unbiased reporting about the events composed at the time whether the events occurred. In addition to that, it states that the command of the 9th Knin Corps was informed about these events.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: This is just the first page or the cover page of the document that I described as a typical, regular, and prescribed document of writing reports within the security service of the JNA. We can see here that the security organ of the 180th motorised brigade, navy captain Simo Rosic, hereby informs his superior within the security organ of the 9th Corps of the data provided by his associate, Ranko, concerning the events in the village of Bruska on the 23rd of October 1992. The content of this report was on the second page typically.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Could the Court clerk kindly show the second page for the general to see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the second page of the same document. Could we see the third page, if we want to discuss the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, please. If the Court clerk might kindly show the third page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is the third page, which says that this is a report on the killing of a large number of civilians who were predominantly members of the Marinovic family. They were killed in Bruska, and in the media in Croatia, or rather what was broadcast in Croatia indicated that this had been perpetrated by the Ustasha forces, which is how the Serbian side always referred to Croatian forces. It is clear that the security organ obtained different information than what was reported by the police station in Obravac [phoen]. Can I see the bottom of the document, please? In the note we see that the security organ writes that the public security station in Benkovac concluded the work on this case when the civilians were killed in Bruska, by concluding that the crime had been committed by the Ustasha sabotage terrorist group, which was a synonym for the Croatian side. The security organ writing this note indicates that the work on this case needs to be continued in order to clear the Serbian side, which is completely illogical in view of the previous conclusion where it was stated that this had been conducted by Serbs because of some old-standing feud. So I conclude that this must be some kind of a slip of tongue because in the last sentence, it should state that this was -- this ought to be done in order to clear the Croatian people of this crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So, according to this you, this document is a blatant attempt to falsify what was actually happening on the ground by the police on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the conclusion of the security organ. I have no reason to disagree with it because later investigations of this case conducted after the war came to the conclusion that this crime had not been perpetrated by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, general, this is a document in essence coming from the security organ and it's a report of the situation in the Sisak/Bajana [phoen] region. In essence, what is the report actually saying? It's from group leader Lieutenant Colonel Tarbuk to his superior in the security organ.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Correct. This is a telegram or a dispatch, as we used to call them in the JNA, in which Colonel Tarbuk informs about the action which took place on the 31st of July 1991, against the police station in Tarkavcani [phoen]. Based on this, we can conclude that the action had been pre-planned and there was an attempt to justify it by staging shootings in the nearby Serbian villages in order to justify this action. I believe that this was done in order to eliminate the police station of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia from that area because they wanted this area to be ethnically pure. What is interesting is that this is the first half of July 1991, when not a single barracks in Croatia was blocked and when there were no -- there was no combat raging in the territory of Croatia which was the case later on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the date was 13th of July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: This is clearly the type of a case, and, if I may add, this was perpetrated with the support of the JNA, because Slobodan Tarbuk was a security officer of the JNA, of a military district of the JNA, and later on a prominent JNA officer in that area. However, in early July 1991, we can see that the JNA supported a creation of such a situation in that area, namely an attack on the legal Croatian police station. Not only did they support such action but also participated in it because Slobodan Tarbuk, here, is identified as a leader of the group.

utterances.text: Now, when this document comes on your screen, General, you'll see that it's a map and it's a map with markings on it which you explained in your testimony in the Milosevic case, which has actually been received into the evidence and is fully described and explained what the markings are in your transcript. So I would simply like you to confirm that this is indeed the map which you made and the markings you made on it, if you could kindly do that.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct. This is the same map that I elaborated on and marked or highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Since an adequate explanation of the various highlightings is made in the transcripts, without any further explanation I would request that the Chamber receive this document as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P87.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, general, we are now going to look at an exhibit which concerns your activities as a negotiator with the JNA. So if I may kindly ask the Court clerk to call up 65 ter 203, bearing ERN 10 -- sorry, my mistake, start again. 01846579 in English and ZA008765 in B/C/S. General, are you able to see this agreement and can you briefly explain to the Court in essence what it is about?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: This is an agreement signed by the Croatian side and the JNA. The agreement was sponsored and mediated by the ECMM in Zagreb. It was signed on the 8th of October 1991. In actual fact, this was the first day of negotiations between the Croatian side and the JNA, the objective being to have an agreement implemented that had been reached by representatives of Croatia and Serbia on the 4th of October 1991. There are several items that we can see here but the most important one is the first one, about a cease-fire to take effect at 1800 hours on that same day. A few items then remain, and, if necessary, I will be glad to explain them. One of the important items is that talks should start immediately about offering assistance to those wounded and ill who were in the Vukovar Hospital. This occurred the next day. They started trying to reach a solution in order to solve that crisis and we are well aware of the results. If I may, another important point here is that there should be immediate talks on evacuating or withdrawing, rather, JNA units from Croatian territory. The barracks should be deblockaded and the units of the JNA should be withdrawn from Croatian territory. These were the essential, the crucial, points of the agreement, which is not to say that the other points were not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And general, can you confirm that you have signed this document and what the date of the document is?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The document was signed on the evening of the 8th of October 1991. It was signed by General Andrija Raseta, Colonel Stjepan Adanic, who was assistant to the Croatian defence minister. I signed the document in my capacity as official negotiator on behalf of the president of the Republic of Croatia and we see the signature of the mediator, the Dutch ambassador, Dirk Jan van Houten, who chaired the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And may I request the Chamber that this document be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P88.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And may I kindly ask the Court clerk to call up 65 ter 507 with English translation 03029257 and B/C/S 02077090.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Are you able to see the document, General?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And you'll see this document is dated 12th of October 1991, which is four days after the cease-fire agreement and it's signed by the chief of the General Staff, Colonel General Adzic. Now, what in essence is this document saying?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: This was a common document, at least as far as the administration for moral guidance was concerned, or as we used to call it, the JNA's political administration. This administration would send these documents to their units down the chain of command. It is typical that this one was signed by the chief of the General Staff which was not frequently the case. Usually it was the chief of the police administration who signed their own reports. But in this case, greater weight is lent to the assessments and tasks detailed in this document. When I familiarised myself with this document during my testimony, what struck me as characteristic, that this was on the 12th of October 1991 which is four days after the signing of the cease-fire in Zagreb, the document that we looked at a while ago. The document specifying that there should be immediate talks arranging a JNA withdrawal from Croatian territory. In this document signed by General Adzic we see that the JNA would not be allowed to leave the Republic of Croatia. This is four days after the previous, original agreement, and yet what we see stated here is of a quite different nature. This is a form of a directive that he passed on to the JNA units, about forcible evacuation of the barracks and combat activities. Could you please scroll down to the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And general I would like to draw, indeed, as you are, your attention to the final paragraph, and, in essence, this seems to be ordering that the volunteer units and TO be put under the single unified command of the JNA. Now, is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Could we just please show the entire document? In the last passage, it starts, "All armed units, regardless of whether components of the JNA, Territorial Defence or volunteer units, must act under the single command of the JNA, meaning the JNA commands in a certain area are hereby being made responsible for all units in the area, and here I mean Serb units, needless to say. Both volunteer units and Territorial Defence. Responsibility here is meant as absolute responsibility, if you ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, General, we earlier looked at some documents regarding a certain massacre in on 18th November, 19th November, which is dated after with this document which is dated 12th of October 1991. So it's quite clear, I think, from this document that the JNA were actually commanding the TO and Serb volunteer detachments and had full knowledge of the crimes which were going on. Now, would that be a correct assessment?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know if the JNA were commanding the TO and Serb volunteer detachments. They should know whether those units obeyed them or not. But it is clear that they had orders from their superiors, in this case the chief of the General Staff, to command those units. That is beyond doubt. Whether those units on the ground obeyed them and followed their orders is not something that I can say. It appears that there were cases of poor coordination where their orders were disobeyed by those on the ground. At least when talking about this period of time. This seems to be an error by the JNA command because they had failed to create the right sort of conditions for those units on the ground to effectively obey them as they had been ordered to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: But nevertheless, in your view, the actions of those units on the ground would be the responsibility of the JNA officers, whether or not they choose to act upon their conduct?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what it means to receive an order from your superior, that appears to be the case. But if you look at the Bruska case, if you look at Nadin and Skabrnja, it is clear that the JNA seems to be reaching different conclusions from those reached by the police when investigating certain incidents so the conclusion seems to be that they had not been obeying them. I suppose the JNA knew that. The necessary thing was to establish a system and for the system to function according to orders received from the chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: May I kindly ask that that document also be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P89.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And may I ask the Court clerk to put up the next document which is 65 ter 204 and unfortunately there is only an English copy of it and it bears ERN 01846645.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, General, this is a document dated 24th of October 1991, which I understand had been read over to you in a language you understand before you testified, and it is a document whereby you are complaining to the EC mission in Zagreb regarding the shelling of Dubrovnik. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the very document. I saw the document in the Croatian original too and this is a document that I wrote at the time. This is one of the many requests, appeals, calls for help, I'm not sure what I should call them, that I sent to General Raseta to ECMM mediators in Zagreb, or whoever else, to stop firing on Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: May I kindly ask for that document to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P90.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And if I may ask the Court clerk to kindly put up document 65 ter 205, bearing ERN ZA002320 in English and B/C/S ZA002319.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: General, do you have a copy of this document?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And this is a document which you sent in your capacity as a member of the negotiating committee to the EC monitoring mission concerning the evacuation of the wounded from Vukovar Hospital on 12th of October 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the first convoy that was organised straight after the signing of the cease-fire agreement that we discussed a while ago, the one dated the 8th of October. Difficulties arose for numerous reasons, but, above all, because an appeal had been sent on account of our concern that the wounded were left in the care, quotation marks, care, of the JNA. We had great concern about what would become of them. Here it was written, "The 12th of October 1991, at 1240 hundred hours" because we had been receiving reports from the convoy on the ground to the effect that there was a great danger of the wounded being massacred by units that were in the area and under their control. That is why an appeal was sent to the European Commission to send in their own observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And can you just clarify, general, who you mean by "their" control?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Having crossed the confrontation line between Croatia and this other side, both on its way to Vukovar and on its way back, the convoy was passing through an area that was under the control of units that were not our units. Therefore, it was moving through a hostile environment and that's why we were concerned about their fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And this hostile environment was one controlled by the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct. It was common, at least that's what had been set out in our request, that all activity in the area, or if they had a request of their own, to do with the activity in Croat-controlled territory, that there should be European community observers in Zagreb as a token of some sort of neutrality. There was the guarantee that we requested in this case for those wounded who were being evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: May I ask the Chamber if this document can be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P91.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: If I could ask the Court clerk to kindly bring up on the screen 65 ter number 206, English translation ZA002321 and in B/C/S, ZA002322.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: General, now, is this a document which you received from General Tus on the 18th of October, concerning the hospital in Vukovar and the fact that it was suffering heavy artillery attacks and in the last couple of days there had been 83 wounded?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Correct. It's a letter sent by the chief of the Main Staff of the Republic of Croatia to the European mission and me personally, in order to inform me about events in Vukovar, specifically the continuing attacks against the hospital and the situation prevailing in the hospital. The letter contains a plea or a request, if you like, to try to get the European mission to intercede with the JNA for these attacks to cease because of the serious situation in the hospital. There is also a request to speed up the evacuation of the wounded and above all to cease the attacks against the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And did these attacks cease?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Based on those talks, I can say that appeals were being sent out on a daily basis by Dr. Vesna Bosanac, by phone. Some were sent to me, some were sent to other Croatian authorities. Some were sent to the chief of the Main Staff. She begged. She cautioned. She called that the firing on the hospital be stopped. She claimed the firing was intense and daily. If I may, I will also tell you about a specific case when I tried to intercede with General Raseta. In an angry tone, because I had been frustrated already with all these appeals that were arriving from Vukovar on a daily basis, I asked that he speak to the General Staff immediately to stop firing on the hospital. The negotiations broke down because they had been interrupted by the mediators. As usual, Raseta went through to a different room. He spoke to someone on the phone and came back, telling the ECMM people and me that just a minute before he had been talking to General Zivota Panic, who was at an observation post from which he had a clear view of the hospital and whatever else was going on in Vukovar. General Panic assured him that there was no firing on the hospital and that the hospital was not being targeted, these being the very words that Raseta used in his report to us, stating in no uncertain terms that the Croatian side was lying. On that same occasion, however, he also mentioned that he had been told by General Panic that there was firing or rather shelling from the hospital itself against their own, that is the JNA positions. This was a paradox and a patent untruth because there simply were no weapons in the hospital, especially no artillery weapons. That much was certain. This indicated to me at the time that General Panic was near Vukovar and in charge of operations one way or another. On the other hand, he justified any firing on the hospital by the fact that their own positions were allegedly being shelled from inside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: May I ask that this document be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P92.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And can I ask the court clerk to call up document 65 ter 207, with English translation, 03369959, and B/C/S 03269959.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And this document, General, concerns the actual proposed evacuation on the 18th of November from the hospital, and it discusses a particular route that should be taken, and also requests the presence of the International Red Cross and monitors. It is written by Franjo Greguriv -- can you tell us please who Franjo Greguriv is?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Franjo Greguriv was the Prime Minister at the time in the so-called coalition government comprising all political parties. The government came into office early in August 1991, replacing the previous government that had been composed solely of members of the HDZ. This document indicates that it was written on the 17th of November 1991 by which time it had become obvious that Vukovar's resistance had either ceased altogether or had become negligible. On the 18th of November 1991, unfortunately, Vukovar was occupied in its entirety. This is exactly 14 years ago. Again, new importance is given to the evacuation of the wounded and ill. There was concern about their fate. That is why a high-ranking official such as Prime Minister addressed General Raseta to start evacuation talks. He also proposed the requirements and conditions that you can see on the face of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: May I ask that this document also be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P93.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And can the Court clerk kindly put up document 65 ter 208, which is B/C/S 03031386 and English 00381397.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, General, is this the copy of the evacuation agreement in respect of the hospital which was signed on 18th November 1991?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: That's correct. This is the agreement which came about based on the Croatian request, and was linked to the previous document that we saw. It was signed by the Minister of Health of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Andrija Hebrang, General Raseta, and the person who acted as a mediator in negotiations was either Ambassador van Houten or Ambassador Cheny [phoen] who substituted for Ambassador van Houten. I don't know which one of them was present. I can't tell based on the signature. This is the agreement specifying how the evacuation of the wounded and ill from the hospital would be organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And did the JNA abide by this evacuation agreement?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: I can say that there was a lot of hesitation, routes were changed on many occasions, and finally the evacuation was conducted via a route that was an alternative one. The JNA did not comply entirely with the agreement. The Croatian side proposed that, in view of the urgency of the situation, the evacuation be conducted via the Danube, which was without any obstacles, and was -- or via helicopters. However, they refused to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: May I ask that this document also be exhibited, though my colleague has drawn to my attention that it's already marked for identification as number 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. So the document marked for identification as number 40 will now become Exhibit 40. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's duly noted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely why I got up. Defence expressed reservations concerning this document, and we still stand by them. We have some concerns concerning the authenticity of the signatures here, and I hope that eventually we would be told everything we want to know following which we would either withdraw our objections or would continue to challenge this document. I hope that we will be provided such pertinent information as soon as possible. For the time being, could this document be just marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Agha, are you content for that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: At this stage I will press for its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Then you will have to explore with the witness whether he can identify the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Indeed, I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: General, is that evacuation agreement still on your screen?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, if I can kindly ask the Court clerk to take us to the signature block and perhaps blow that up, can you recognise any of those signatures there and which ones?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: The signature on the left is definitely the signature of Minister Hebrang. The one on the right I'm almost fully certain is a signature of General Andrija Raseta because this is how he used to sign his name. The document -- the signature in the middle is that of the mediator, and I believe that this was the French ambassador, Cheny who was the deputy of the presiding chairman of the European mission, Ambassador Van Houten. Occasionally, he used to chair negotiations. It seems to me that precisely during that time, Ambassador van Houten was ill and was in the former military hospital in Zagreb, where they -- where he underwent kidney treatment. This is why I believe the signature to be that of Ambassador Cheny.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you for a moment you were obviously working closely with the Croatian Defence Minister Hebrang so you would be familiar with his signature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it hundreds of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And you also had numerous dealings with General Raseta as your counterpart so you would be familiar with that signature as well, I take it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let us try and compare the signature on the document dated the 8th of October 1991 with this signature, if technically feasible, and I think the situation will be clear to us. We have the signature of Raseta on the document of the 8 October, the one that was just exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, would the Chamber care to make a comparison or is this sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I be given an opportunity to say something that my learned friend from the Prosecution is probably familiar with? Namely, General Raseta, the one mentioned here, gave a statement to the OTP investigators, in which he said that there had been negotiations but that they failed to reach an agreement, and that he never signed such an agreement. This is one of the basic reasons that prompted the Defence to verify these claims. Perhaps my learned friends can confirm that they do indeed have such a statement and that this was stated there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have reached the point, Mr. Agha, and Mr. Vasic, when we must break because the tape is about to finish, and it seems to the Chamber to be an ideal opportunity, given the weekend that lies ahead, for there to be further discussions between you with regard to the information that had been indicated earlier, I believe, by Mr. Moore, would be made available to the Defence about this document. And when we resume on Monday, no doubt, the Chamber will learn from you the outcome of your discussions and any information that might be further available, and it -- if there is no satisfactory resolution of that, it will be in Mr. Agha's hands whether he pursues further at the moment the question of these signatures and this document or whether some other proof will be offered. And we will deal with that then. So, for the moment, the document, despite what I said a little earlier before hearing Mr. Vasic, will remain marked for identification only as 40, and we hope that it will be proved possible by Monday to deal with this issue in a satisfactory manner. I'm sorry, General, but we have run to the end of our time for today and we will resume again on Monday. We must ask you to return then, and we resume on Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of November, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
